headline: Eiji is 英 (ei, “English”) plus 字 (ji, “character, letter”).
Toho is a Sino-Japanese word from 徒步, maybe from Middle Chinese.
Kikon is 既 (ki, “already”) plus 婚 (kon, “marriage”).
Sōdai is from Middle Chinese 壮大 (MC dajH|daH).
Orimono is 織り (ori, the stem of 織る (oru), weaving, woven) plus 物 (mono, “thing”).
ビジネス is from English business.
Kottōhin is, by surface analysis, 骨董 (kottō) plus 品 (-hin).
Kokorozuyoi is 心 (kokoro, “heart, feelings”) plus 強い (tsuyoi, “strong”), with tsuyoi voiced to zuyoi by rendaku.
Mabataki is the continuative stem of the verb 瞬く (matataku, “to blink”).
カムバック is from English comeback, and its idol fandom sense is a semantic loan from Korean.
Hōsha is a calque of English radiation.
Nayamashii is from the verb 悩む (nayamu) and the adjectivizing suffix しい (-shii).
Ōmizu is 大 (ō, “great”) plus 水 (mizu, “water”).
Arasoi is the continuative stem of the verb 争う (arasō, “to compete, argue”).
Kogara is 小 (ko-, “little”) plus 柄 (gara, “physique, build”).
Mokuromi is the continuative stem of the verb 目論む (mokuromu).
Ronri is from the Middle Chinese compound 論理, literally “debate, theory + reason, principle”.
チーム is from English team.
Tamashii is 魂 (tama, “soul, spirit”) plus an uncertain shii, possibly 強ひ (shihi), from the classical verb 強ふ.
Jitsugyōka is, by surface analysis, 実業 (jitsugyō) plus 家 (-ka).
Otoroeru is from Classical Japanese 衰ふ (otorofu), 劣ろ (otoro, the irrealis of 劣る (otoru, “to be inferior to”)) plus ふ (-fu).
ファン is borrowed from English fan.
コマーシャル is borrowed from English commercial.
Mihakarau is 見る (miru, “to see”) plus 計らう (hakarau, “to arrange, take measures”).
Daiben is 大 (“big”) plus 便 (“excreta”).
Jigoku is from Middle Chinese 地獄, literally “(under)ground prison”.
Hateru is from Old Japanese はつ (patu), a lower bigrade verb.
クイズ is borrowed from English quiz.
The kanji of mucha are ateji, literally meaning “tealess”.
Minoue is 身 (mi) plus の (no) plus 上 (ue).
Omomuku was originally 面向く (omomuku), 面 (omo, “face”) plus 向く (muku, “toward”).
